title: Initial Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Authentication Scheme Registrations
summary: Registers HTTP authentication schemes that were defined in RFCs before the IANA HTTP Authentication Scheme Registry existed, so the registry has an initial set of entries.

plainLanguage.summary: A new list of ways to prove who you are was started, and this document writes the older, already existing ways onto it.

questions: which http auth schemes are registered
subtitle: Registry entries for HTTP authentication mechanisms

tldr.problem: HTTP authentication schemes were defined in multiple RFCs before an IANA registry for them existed, so the registry needed an initial set of entries.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC formally registers the existing HTTP authentication schemes (Basic, Bearer, Digest, Negotiate, and OAuth) in the IANA HTTP Authentication Scheme Registry.
tldr.outcome: The registry now has a complete record of standard HTTP authentication methods, making it official reference for which schemes are registered.

today: RFC 7236 is an Informational Standard that documents the initial entries in the IANA HTTP Authentication Scheme Registry. The registry continues to be maintained at IANA for new scheme registrations.

sections.title: Registering Existing Authentication Schemes
sections.content:
HTTP clients and servers use authentication schemes to verify user identity. The most common are Basic Authentication and Digest Authentication, defined decades ago in RFC 2617. When IANA created the HTTP Authentication Scheme Registry, the existing schemes needed to be formally registered.

This RFC registers five schemes: Basic, Bearer, Digest, Negotiate, and OAuth. Each registration points to the RFC that defines it, creating a complete official record.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP has several ways to prove who you are. This document puts them all in an official list.

sections.title: The Registered Schemes
sections.content: Basic and Digest Authentication come from RFC 2617. Bearer tokens are from RFC 6750, used for OAuth 2.0. Negotiate is from RFC 4559, for Kerberos and NTLM authentication in Windows environments. OAuth (version 1.0) comes from RFC 5849. Each has a reference note; Negotiate is flagged as violating HTTP semantics by being connection-oriented rather than stateless.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five main ways to prove you are who you say you are in HTTP: passwords, hashed passwords, bearer tokens, Kerberos, and OAuth.

sections.title: Why the Registry Matters
sections.content: The registry prevents duplicate or conflicting scheme names and provides a reference point for HTTP implementations. Developers can check the registry to see what schemes are official. The registration of existing schemes ensures continuity: these methods are already widely deployed, and the registry codifies their status. Future new schemes must also be registered here.
sections.plainLanguage: An official list means everyone knows which authentication methods are real and which are made up.

references.text: Franks, J., Hallam-Baker, P., Hostetler, J., Lawrence, S., Leach, P., Luotonen, A., and L. Stewart, "HTTP Authentication: Basic and Digest Access Authentication", RFC 2617, June 1999.
